1:
The Greek heading of this psalm turns out to matter. Keil and Delitzsch report that the old Greek version renders the inscription unto the end, for those that shall be changed — which they call unintelligible and ungrammatical — a testimony to Asaph, a psalm concerning the Assyrian; and they hold the last clause important, since as an ancient interpretive note it solves the riddle why Joseph should represent all Israel here and why the tribes of Joseph in particular are named. Augustine of Hippo is found working from precisely that heading, quoting each of its clauses in turn as the title of his psalm; and where Keil and Delitzsch take the last as a historical hint, Augustine turns it into a moral category by etymology, since the name of that nation is interpreted as men guiding, so that what is addressed is no longer a generation which has not guided its heart but a generation guiding. He reads the whole as a song of the Advent and of the vineyard, that is, of head and body, king and people, shepherd and flock.

Why three particular tribes are named divides them further. John Calvin holds the psalm composed on behalf of the ten tribes after that kingdom began to be wasted, and it is not without reason, he says, that Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh are expressly mentioned; the paragraph attached to his block then supplies a rival explanation at length from the order of the march in the wilderness, where those three tribes followed immediately behind the ark. John Gill and John Wesley give the same marching order. Charles Ellicott presses that explanation into an argument against Calvin’s: the tribes encamped side by side and headed the procession, and the preposition before would alone show that this ancient arrangement and no recent political event determines the way the poet introduces them, so that it is very doubtful whether the choice of Joseph is a distinct reference to the northern kingdom at all. Adam Clarke reports a fourth view, that the three simply stand for the whole, one being absorbed into Judah, one comprehending the country beyond the river and one representing all the rest. Clarke also states the psalm’s architecture exactly, that there are four parts in it, three closing with the same refrain and the fourth with words nearly the same.

On the title given to God, Ellicott distributes the patriarchal names: shepherd and rock were the especial names of one patriarch for God, as fear was of another and mighty of a third, and in the blessing of Joseph the first made more than usually solemn pronunciation of it. C.H. Spurgeon reaches the same place independently, that the dying words of that patriarch may be what the verse refers to, and adds that broken hearts delight in names of grace. On the cherubim between which God is said to dwell, Ellicott insists the picture is drawn not from clouds but from the sculptured wings above the ark. Clarke prefers to note that a Hebrew lexicon of his day gives about twenty quarto pages to those symbolic beings, which he calls a long and painful account, or system of conjectures. Matthew Henry makes the same seat theological, since the mercy-seat stood there and it is comfortable to look up to God as sitting on a throne of grace, which he is to us only because of the great propitiation. Clarke adds a manuscript curiosity, that one old copy at Cambridge writes this psalm and the one before it as a single psalm.
4:
That God should be angry with the prayer itself is felt as the sharpest thing here, and two of them independently reach the same image for it. C.H. Spurgeon asks how long the smoke of God’s wrath shall drown the smoking incense of the people’s prayers, since prayer would gladly enter the holy place but is met and prevented by that wrath; and he observes that anger against sinners seems natural enough, but anger against their praying is a bitter grief. Charles Ellicott arrives at the same picture by grammar rather than by feeling: the verb means literally to have fumed, in a construction that combines two clauses so that the sense is thou hast been long angry, how long wilt thou continue; and the preposition is not against but during the prayer, the smoke of the divine anger being conceived perhaps as a cloud through which the ascending incense of petition cannot penetrate. Keil and Delitzsch mark what the strophe is doing rather than what it says, that the complaint here becomes detailed by contrasting the former days with the present, and that the prayer grows more importunate in step with it.

On the bread of tears John Gill gives two senses, tears instead of bread where there is none to eat, or bread mingled and dipped in them. Spurgeon expands the second: their meat is seasoned with brine distilled from weeping eyes, and meals that were once seasons of social merriment are now like funeral feasts to which each man contributes his bitter morsel. The measure named in the same verse is disputed three ways. Adam Clarke renders the word threefold and reports that some take it for a particular measure used by the captors, whose capacity is not known, while others make it simply abundance. Ellicott derives it from a third part and suggests a third of a standard measure, but holds it evidently used here in a general way, as we might speak of a peck of troubles.

The complaint that they are made a strife to their neighbours is read three ways. Gill offers either that they are forced to contend for their own defence, or that having been given into their enemies’ hands those enemies now quarrel among themselves over dividing the spoil. Clarke offers a subtler first sense, that the neighbouring peoples have a controversy about them, a nation so wonderfully preserved and so wonderfully punished being a mystery to them, in whom they see both the goodness and the severity of God; his alternative is the plain one, that all the surrounding nations join to malign and execrate them. Ellicott admits only that plain sense, saying they could be a strife to their neighbours in no other. He adds that the last clause reads literally that the enemies laugh for themselves, though the older versions have them laughing at us. Gill closes the section by noting what the repeated refrain shows, namely what was uppermost in the minds of that people and what they were most desirous of, the light of God’s countenance.
8:
Where the figure of the vine came from interests two of them. Charles Ellicott holds it so natural and apt that its repetition through the older books and its adoption in the newer is no surprise, and guesses that the song of the vineyard in one prophet was the parent image, unless the patriarchal blessing on Joseph suggested that song in turn; Keil and Delitzsch reach for the same blessing, where Joseph is compared to the layer of a fruitful growth whose shoots climb over a wall. Adam Clarke instead catalogues the users, naming five prophets, the lawgiver and Christ himself, and calls it the ordinary figure for that people. Ellicott adds a fine grammatical point about the verb: it is to be taken as a historic present, and it serves both for horticulture and for breaking up a nomadic camp, pulling out the tent-pins and driving them in again elsewhere, so that transplanting a vine and striking a camp are one word.

Clarke then runs the horticulture as a numbered allegory across five verses. First the vine is brought out of a worse soil into a better. Second, the husbandman hews down and roots up the other trees and gathers out the stones and brambles that would choke the young vines, as the nations were cast out of the land. Third, the ground is dug and manured and the vines set at proper distances, answering to the division of the land by lot. Fourth, they are sheltered, propped and loosened about the root so as to take firm hold. Fifth, to multiply his stock the gardener cuts a shoot with a joint at either end, of which the lower furnishes roots and the upper the new growth, so that one tree soon makes a whole vineyard. Sixth, the grown vine spreads to any extent and makes shade under which men not only shelter but eat and dwell. Seventh, the vineyard is fenced against trampling and against the passer-by, which is why the psalm can ask why the hedges are broken down. He ends with the technical note that vines are propagated not only by cuttings but by layers, seed, grafting and inoculation.

On the extent reached, John Wesley, Ellicott and Clarke agree that the sea and the river are the western sea and the great eastern river, the limits of the empire at its height. C.H. Spurgeon supplies the clearing that made room, with the old trees that had long engrossed the soil torn up root and branch. Matthew Henry draws the character of the plant itself, weak and needing support, unsightly and of unpromising outside, yet spreading and fruitful and its fruit most excellent. John Gill notes the paradox of its beginning, that the more it was afflicted in the first country the more it grew. On the broken hedge Gill names what the fence was, the angels that encamp about God’s people, and salvation as walls and bulwarks, and God himself as a wall of fire. The boar that follows is identified three ways in Gill’s note alone: as the Assyrian king who carried the ten tribes away, for which he cites the same Greek heading of the psalm that others use to date it; as a later persecutor, on one scholar’s reading; and by Jewish interpreters as the fourth beast, meaning the Roman empire. Ellicott meanwhile keeps to the words, rendering the ninth verse as striking its roots deep and observing that the goodly cedars are literally cedars of God, the branches of a vine being asked to match the luxuriance of the most magnificent of forest trees.
14:
The word rendered vineyard occurs nowhere else, and John Gill collects what has been made of it. Its first letter is written larger than usual in the copies, which some take as a perpetual memorial of the bringing of the vine out of Egypt, and its crooked shape as a hint of that vine’s later oppression. One Aramaic version renders the word a branch or shoot, one Jewish commentator a plant, others a habitation, and another treats it as an adjective meaning established; Gill himself calls it an Egyptian word for a plant, and notes that the ivy was for the same reason named by the Greeks after one of their gods. Charles Ellicott reports that most modern scholars follow the two oldest versions in making it not a noun at all but the imperative of a verb meaning protect, so that the line reads protect what thy right hand hath planted — which, he adds, makes a good parallelism.

Ellicott then does something more drastic, and rearranges the closing section. The verse about burning and cutting down would be far more intelligible, and would fit the rhythm better, if it followed immediately upon the verse about the boar and the wild beast, since the poet, having just complained that God fumed with anger during their prayer, would scarcely speak of his own people as perishing at his rebuke; read in that order, the beasts are what perish. And the verse about the man of the right hand, he says, is manifestly a continuation of the verse about the vineyard and should follow it, so that the request to protect what the right hand planted is answered by the request that the hand be laid over the man of the right hand. He prints both rearrangements in full.

Who that man is divides them three to two. Adam Clarke argues it from the text: the original of the earlier verse speaks of the Son whom thou hast strengthened, an Aramaic version renders it the King Messiah outright, five ancient versions read son of man, and eighteen manuscripts of two collators read the same, so that this was probably the reading of the original copies — from which Clarke draws a large conclusion, that since Christ seems to be intended, this is the first place in the older scriptures where that title is applied to him. He adds that an old English psalter understood the verse of Christ being set at God’s right hand, and that no one else can be said to stand there as intercessor. Gill reports three candidates, the people at large, the reigning king as the vineyard’s keeper, and the Messiah, and prefers the last on the authority of three Jewish interpreters, one of whom allows either the nation or a messiah descended from Joseph. Matthew Henry agrees and makes him the arm of the Lord, concluding that the vine therefore cannot be ruined. Ellicott denies it flatly: some see a reference to the Messiah in the words son and son of man, but the parallelism and context show the poet to be thinking of the nation as a community, of which the vine is the emblem. John Wesley takes the same side, glossing son of man as the people, who are often spoken of as one person. Gill closes by noticing that the refrain grows as it returns, addressing first God, then the God of hosts, then the Lord God of hosts; some, he says, have found the Trinity suggested there, which he thinks a better thought than the reading that counts three captivities.
